One of the Best introductions to the process of Writing (Sci-fi/Fantasy) I've ever encountered
This lecture series is inspiring me to write, and I wanted to encourage those interested in writing to check it out and give your thoughts.
This is excellent. I love Sanderson's books and I never looked at writing this way before. I'm planning on being an author myself so this video was a nice treat, thank you for sharing :)

Just dealing with this video, as I haven't watched any of the others. Sanderson is throwing most students under the bus when it comes to learning writing. He actively states that practice is this magic "one-step" path to good writing, when it really is a part of a larger process. Sure, practice is important, but experience doesn't equal understanding. Understanding comes from studying both variety and self-editing. To use one of his analogies, the batter gains the muscle memory to successfully swing and hit a ball from practice, but it isn't solely based on this. If the batter practiced on hitting curve-balls only, he would be unprepared (in some cases dangerously so) for a straight. Sure, muscle memory would carry him a certain distance, but ultimately he is less capable of hitting a ball than someone who practiced hitting a variety of pitches. Self-editing in this case would take the shape of keeping good form. A batter who has sloppy form may be able to bunt or get a hit, but without proper form, I find it unlikely that they'll ever get a home-run (for the record, this isn't always the goal of a batter at plate.) In the same way, editing your style and learning about new styles helps develop a better writer.

He also states that if you aren't interested in short stories that it would be a disservice to write them. From a learning standpoint, this is akin to telling a math student who is interested in algebra to ignore basic math because that isn't their goal. Learning about and writing short stories is just as structurally important as learning basic math, and when you do get up to higher levels, it aids in making that easier to master. A short story, at the start of a writing apprenticeship, is just as unruly a beast as any novella or novel. The plots buckle, the characters are flat, the structure and style are pathetic. Unlike a novella or novel though, a short story is short. You can sit down and read over it for editing significantly faster. You can learn about what tightens up a plot, how to bring characters to life, and how to make sure you hit points with the story that will resonate with readers. All in a neat 3k to 5k box. Sanderson is asking his students to fight a dragon when some kobolds will do. That's the real disservice.

Apparently (although this is my opinion) Sanderson doesn't know the difference between metaphors and analogies. Both examples he gives, the batter and discerning a good pianist, are not metaphors. He is drawing similarities between two separate ideas to attempt a smoother transition into discussing writing-- an analogy. A metaphor would be if he were to have said, "Writing is music. When you hit the right notes in order, your music is going to flow beautifully and people will want to hear it. When you mix up the notes, people are going to cover their ears." That's a metaphor. I can't understand how a published author and educator in this specific field can mess that up.

Take what he says and even what I have written how you will. Writing is an art-form and subject to perception. If you want to view learning how to write differently than either of us, go for it. Develop yourself and your style. But please don't put this forward as anywhere near the "end-all, be-all" of learning writing. You get what you pay for, and in Sanderson's case, it's not enough.

I appreciate you taking the time to put your thoughts to page. You should be aware that the class was about writing novels. You are right about practice isn't the end all be all for achieving excellence. Skill is critical however and practice more than any other factor is the method to get to those ends. I can practice my jump shot for 10,000 hours, but I'll never get in the NBA, period; so I do get your sentiment. And my impression is that that sentiment is what Sanderson was getting at when choosing a writing platform. If you're inclined to write novels, learn to write a novel; if you're a short story person, write short stories. I myself can't write a short story well either; so I can see where the thought is coming from. It's not to say however that making attempts at short stories are fruitless if you intend to write novels. The way I was taught in particular, and GRRM said it best at a seminar once, "I just crash 40 short stories together into a thing you all read". The writing in this method then is about managing a series of networks of events that all coalesce into a proper fully articulated story. Sanderson does bring bestselling authors in to discuss this very methodology. Here is the entire class syllabus to give you a perspective on the entire lecture series. He was articulating that that is not how HE does it, but he does explain in depth, the differences between his approach and other successful writers.

As for analogies vs metaphors, to be so simplistic in the metaphor vs analogy sphere is a disservice to the communication I believe. They are often used together when discussing both creative design and creative writing and blurred lines between these concepts exist, if not from an appropriate linguistic perspective, they certainly do in the reality of written and discussed form. When listening to a piano player, I can ascertain, even though I can not play the instrument, the skill level of the player. He says clearly that this is an equivalent to assessing a writer. That was his point. That sounds like a metaphor for skills assessment when considered that way to me. He is not drawing similarities, he is saying it's the same. In fact, he says those exact words at 2:26 into the 1st video. I can see your point though. He is not saying Skill in Assessing Musical Ability is Skill in Assessing Writing Ability. He is saying they are the same concept. I think sometimes, we use semantics to ignore the substance of a message, and really, the crux of his communication was that you intrinsically know whether or not writing is good. A fair and accurate point I believe, even if his command of terminology and my understanding of it may indeed be flawed.

Do you have some methodologies to share that might help shed light on a better approach or a different one to Sanderson's? I myself am new to the idea of writing a novel. I am writing my first one as we speak; so I'm inclined to gather as much knowledge about being disciplined to do it effectively as I can.

Disclaimer: Everything from this point on is opinion. Please work toward what you feel is the correct answers in writing.

As I said, the metaphors vs analogies thing was my opinion. I was mostly just peeved that someone with as much experience and training as him confused terminologies for two terms, that while often blurred, are distinct in their usage. I didn't really want to make contentions about his examples, but I don't think assessing skill works in the way Sanderson thinks it does. You could take one look at famous contemporary authors such as McCarthy, Murakami, or even J.K. Rowling and in seconds note that their styles are very dissimilar to each other. Does that mean that they are not all good styles of writing? If I don't like one, does that make them a bad writer? No, and in that way Sanderson is standing there puffing up a poor methodology for looking at writing in general. You can't decipher if writing is good or not based on 1 page. This also doesn't mean that their writings styles are clean and perfect. GRRM (although vastly famous at this point) had what I would consider a very shaky style when he got Game of Thrones published. Does that mean that an editor should have read a single page and chucked the manuscript in a fire? No.

What I'm trying to get at is that for a new writer (or even someone as practiced as Asimov, Martin, Tolkien, etc.) what is really important is exposure and reflection. Anyone who writes shouldn't insulate themselves, but should try to seek out new writing styles, new experiences, and new avenues of ideas as much as possible. The simplest way of going about this is to read. Not just in your style or genre, but as much content that you can get while you prepare yourself to work. Read Seuss; read Tolstoy; read Hemingway and Miller (yes I mean the comic writer.) Watch film, cartoons, and documentaries. Go out and stare at people across the room, listen to their conversations, watch their movements and emotions pour out of them. Read the dictionary once and a while. After you've done stuff (or even while you are still doing it,) write. Put thoughts to page and keep it up until you feel its finished.

Then reflect on it. Read it over and over again. Cut what doesn't fit or what you think people won't want to hear. It doesn't matter. What matters is that in this reflection you find a way to develop your style into something closer to the ideal writer you want to be. If that happens to change over time, let it. Some writers look at 1st drafts and love them. Some run through a draft 5 or 6 times and then scrap the project to start again.

My purpose in pushing short stories isn't about whether or not anyone is good at them, or should get good at them. I'm simply pushing a fact that short stories are shorter. When you are trying to learn about the 'basics' (which nothing about writing is to be fair,) going over a 5,000 word short story is a lot faster than doing the same to a 20,000 word novella or 50,000 word novel. Whether it is good or bad doesn't matter. When you are constrained on time (as the students in this class undoubtedly are) having them run through a few short stories to at least get a little practice on forming structure and style or crafting characters is more helpful than not. It's never meant to make you better at "free-throws," but get you in the form of taking shots when you need to. Whether that's right under the hoop or half-way across the court. The locations are different, but having that understanding of how to shoot makes taking it so much easier.

Again, I make the point that this is all subjective. On the topics of Art, Literature, Film, and everything else involved in aesthetics, making your mark is more a personal journey than an educational opportunity. In this regard, I'm no better than Sanderson in saying anything on the topic. It's my opinion, and having the disclaimer as such above everything in this sub-verse outside of clear and present facts about the business-side of writing should be taken with as much salt as possible.
